1.pericope_label: Praise ye the LORD. O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever... Remember me, O LORD, with the favour that thou bearest unto thy people

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the opening formula as a liturgical refrain holding the place in the Jewish church that the Gloria Patri holds in Christian worship, undatable in its origin but attested by the chronicler at the bringing up of the ark and again at the dedication of the temple, and passing into general use after the Captivity; he also finds in the tone of the fifth verse a prospect of good near at hand which helps fix the psalm's date. Delitzsch turns the chronicler's use of the first and last verses into an argument: since these were already in David's mouth for him, the psalm is no more Maccabean than the two before it, the Psalter must already have stood in five books marked off by doxologies, and the closing benediction must already have been read as part of the psalm.

Gill widens the mighty acts beyond the deliverance from Egypt, to which a Jewish commentator had confined them, taking in creation, providence and redemption; he gives two senses of keeping judgment, either observing God's judgments on the wicked or keeping his statutes as the rule of life, and expands the good of the chosen into the blessings laid up for them rather than any goodness of their own. Calvin states the psalm's relation to the one before it — there God is shown more than a bountiful father, here his benefits are acknowledged turned to bad account — and insists it is not reproof so much as confession offered to obtain pardon, which is why it opens with praise; he also notes that the first and last verses belong to the psalm David gave to Asaph, so that this one has been ascribed to him.

Clarke reports that eminent commentators take the psalm for a prayer of the captives in Babylon, sets the third verse beside its Anglo-Saxon and old Scottish renderings to show how near the older English stands to our own, and prefers the plural reading of the prayer that follows — remember us, that we may rejoice — on the authority of several manuscripts and all the versions but one, as more agreeable to the context. Wesley keeps the singular but has the psalmist speaking for the whole nation, and glosses the seeing of the fifth verse as enjoyment.

Henry answers the question of the second verse by saying the acts are too many to number and too mysterious to describe, that not the angels can show forth all, and that this does not excuse us from doing what we can but should quicken us to do all we can; on the beatitude he has the blessed adhering to the rules of wisdom and religion, just to God and men, and steady at every turn. Spurgeon turns the opening call on his own congregations: it is not fitting for a few to praise while the rest are silent, and if David were present where choirs carry all the singing he would turn to the people and tell them to praise the Lord.

Augustine reports a dispute over the doubled Hallelujah, whether one of the two closes the previous psalm rather than opening this, and declines to settle it against the general custom of attaching the word to whichever psalm it heads, noting that very few copies — and none of the Greek he inspected — place it at the end of the last psalm of all.

debates.question: When was the psalm written, and by whom?

positions.view: A prayer of the captives in Babylon, on the judgment of eminent commentators.
Ascribed to David, since the first and last verses belong to the psalm he delivered to Asaph to be sung before the ark.
No more Maccabean than the neighbouring psalms, since the chronicler already had these verses; and the Psalter already stood in five books marked by doxologies in his day.
The tone of the fifth verse, with its prospect of good near at hand, itself gives a probable date.
Not raised; the psalm begins as the one before it ended, and the question is what the acts are and who may praise them.

debates.question: Is the prayer of the fourth verse singular or plural?

positions.view: Plural, on the authority of several manuscripts and all the versions but one, and as more agreeable to the context: remember us, that we may rejoice.
Singular as it stands, but spoken in the name and on behalf of the whole nation.
Singular and personal, a request to be remembered with the peculiar favour God bears his people.

outliers.note: Reads the opening call as a rebuke of choral performance in his own churches: if David were present where quartettes and choirs carry all the singing, he would turn to the congregation and tell them to praise the Lord.
Prints the third verse in Anglo-Saxon and old Scottish to show how little the English of the beatitude has changed.

themes: Praise ye the Lord. O give thanks unto the Lord; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
Who can utter the mighty acts of the Lord? who can shew forth all his praise?
Blessed are they that keep judgment, and he that doeth righteousness at all times.
Remember me, O Lord, with the favour that thou bearest unto thy people: O visit me with thy salvation;
That I may see the good of thy chosen, that I may rejoice in the gladness of thy nation, that I may glory with thine inheritance.

6.pericope_label: We have sinned with our fathers, we have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly... Then believed they his words; they sang his praise

schools.summary: Ellicott insists that the confession takes in the speaker and his own generation as much as the ancestors, and dates the psalm from the Captivity, when the national conscience — at least in the nobler part of the nation — was thoroughly alive to the sinfulness of idolatry. Delitzsch makes the failure of the seventh verse the root of all that follows: falling away from faith in the promise, they forgot the works done to confirm it; and he treats the singing at the sea and the forgetting that follows as halves of one movement.

Gill traces the inherited guilt back past the immediate fathers to the corrupt nature derived from the first father of all; he notes that they saw the plagues and had no heart to perceive what they were for, and finds the same slowness in the disciples of Christ. On the deliverance he denies any worth in the people and grounds it wholly in the covenant and the name called upon them, adding that spiritual Israel is saved on the same terms; and he is explicit that the belief recorded at the end is noted to show the slowness of their hearts, since they believed only on sight, as Thomas did.

Clarke keeps the generations parallel and distinct — our forefathers sinned and suffered, and we, like them, have sinned and do suffer — reports a rabbinic reading that finds two separate faults in the doubled mention of the sea, puts the ground of the deliverance compactly (there was nothing in them from which God could draw a reason, so he drew it from himself), quotes an old English psalter's retelling of the crossing, and observes that in this psalmist everything has life, the sea behaving proudly, being rebuked, and retiring in confusion. Wesley makes the vindication of the name defensive, that it would have suffered blasphemous reproach had the people been destroyed.

Henry reads the confession as seasonable because the church was in distress: we must justify God in what he brings on us, and the remembrance that former sins did not make him cast off his people is itself ground for hope. Spurgeon makes the sharing formal — Israel was one nation through all time, so the sin confessed is national rather than personal, and a people enjoying national privileges shared national guilt — and notes that the confession is made three times over as a token of sincerity.

positions.view: Two generations kept parallel and distinct: the fathers sinned and suffered, and we in our turn have done the same.
The speaker and his own generation as much as the ancestors, the confession belonging to the Captivity.
National rather than personal sin: Israel was one nation through all time, and those who shared its privileges shared its guilt.
A guilt reaching further back than the immediate fathers, to the corrupt nature derived from the first man.
An addition to the stock of hereditary guilt, filling up the measure of the fathers' iniquity.

debates.question: What does the doubled mention of the sea signify?

positions.view: Two separate faults, on a rabbinic reading: murmuring when the water lay ahead and Pharaoh behind, and then fearing to enter lest they stick fast in the mud.
One failure only, and the root of all that follows: they forgot the works done to confirm the promise.
Not pressed; the point is that they saw the wonders and had no heart to understand them.

outliers.note: Quotes an old English psalter's account of the crossing which appears to suppose the sea divided into twelve separate passages, one for each tribe.
Reads the threefold form of the confession as a model, wanting sins of omission, commission and rebellion acknowledged under distinct heads.

themes: We have sinned with our fathers, we have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly.
Our fathers understood not thy wonders in Egypt; they remembered not the multitude of thy mercies; but provoked him at the sea, even at the Red sea.
Nevertheless he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make his mighty power to be known.
He rebuked the Red sea also, and it was dried up: so he led them through the depths, as through the wilderness.
And he saved them from the hand of him that hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.
And the waters covered their enemies: there was not one of them left.
Then believed they his words; they sang his praise.

13.pericope_label: They soon forgat his works; they waited not for his counsel... had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers the reading of the Greek, Latin and Syriac at the fifteenth verse, satiety rather than leanness, observing that with the other noun taken as lust the verse falls into two parallel clauses; he finds the objection to Moses and Aaron in the title of holiness, which the disaffected held belonged to the whole congregation, and notes that Korah is passed over here in keeping with accounts that distinguish both his attitude and his fate. He uses the same verses as evidence of sources, the phrase for Horeb and the word for the likeness being Deuteronomic; and he offers an alternative to the usual explanation of standing in the breach, that Moses stood submissively before God in the breaking forth of his anger. Delitzsch groups the first three verses as one movement, the earliest of the principal sins beyond the sea being an unthankful and unbelieving murmuring over meat and drink.

Gill fixes the forgetting at three days and notes the margin's reading that they made haste; he distinguishes the craving from natural appetite, which would not be criminal, supplies the claim behind the envy — that Dathan and Abiram, being of Reuben, thought themselves better entitled as sons of Jacob's firstborn — and presses two aggravations at the calf, that the figure was borrowed from the Egyptians who had used them ill and whose judgments they had watched, and that it was made at the mountain where the law against graven images had been given.

Clarke fixes the forgetting at Marah, reads the leanness physically (they despised the manna as innutritive, God gave the flesh without a blessing, and they grew lean rather than fat on it), and uses the word rendered chosen to enter a caution of his own: it would be very difficult to show that this word anywhere in the Old Testament refers to any man's eternal state, much less to unconditional election and reprobation. Wesley also fixes three days, puts the leanness in the body, reads the rebellion as aimed past Aaron at the God who consecrated him, sharpens the exchange at the calf into an ox that must be fed by the people the true God had fed, and adopts the besieged-town sense of standing in the breach.

Henry calls the passage an abridgment of Israel's provocations, abridged again by the apostle for Christians, and treats the margin's making haste as possibly a second fault, their expectations running ahead of God's promises. Spurgeon describes a hurry to get the Lord's mercies out of memory, is most searching on the envy — they owed Moses everything and grudged him the authority he had to exercise for their good, and if the meekest of men was envied who can hope to escape — and notes that the ox is called a calf in scorn, which he holds is never more legitimately used than against attempts to set forth the Invisible God.

debates.question: Is the fifteenth verse about leanness or satiety?

positions.view: Satiety, with the Greek, Latin and Syriac; taking the other noun as lust yields two exact parallel clauses.
Leanness, and physically: they despised the manna, God gave flesh without a blessing, and they grew lean on it.
Leanness in the body, the desire to pamper it becoming the means of destroying it.
Not pressed; the point is that the craving was voluptuous rather than natural, and so criminal.

debates.question: What does it mean that Moses stood in the breach?

positions.view: An image from the defence of a besieged town: God had walled them in, their sins made the breach, and the enemy might have entered but for the intercession.

Possibly rather that Moses stood submissively before God in the breaking forth of his anger, the noun coming from the verb used of the Lord breaking forth upon the people, as the Greek seems to have read it.
Not the phrase but the word chosen is at issue, which cannot be pressed into any doctrine of election.

outliers.note: Uses the description of Moses as God's chosen to deny that the word anywhere in the Old Testament bears on any man's eternal state, much less on unconditional election and reprobation.
Turns the calf into an attack on the ritualists of his own day, whose worship he says is sensuous to the highest degree and appeals to eye, ear and nose.

themes: They soon forgat his works; they waited not for his counsel:
But lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tempted God in the desert.
And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul.
They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron the saint of the Lord.
The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram.
And a fire was kindled in their company; the flame burned up the wicked.
They made a calf in Horeb, and worshipped the molten image.
Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass.
They forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt;
Wondrous works in the land of Ham, and terrible things by the Red sea.
Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them.

24.pericope_label: Yea, they despised the pleasant land, they believed not his word... Because they provoked his spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his lips

schools.summary: Ellicott is careful that the raised hand is lifted not to strike but to give emphasis to an oath, observes that the following verse is evidently copied from a prophet with the prophet's verb scatter replaced by the overthrow just used — an error, if it is one, as old as the Greek — takes the sacrifices of the dead for the sacrifices of a dead divinity rather than any rite for the departed, reports that the versions do not agree even on the verb used of Phinehas, and reads the provoked spirit of the last verse as God's rather than Moses', adding that the usual account of Moses' offence is partial, since the narratives suggest he was excluded less for calling them rebels than for a momentary lapse into their own despairing temper. Delitzsch passes over the whole stretch, running his quotation from the murmuring to the sins in Canaan before commenting.

Gill sets Baal-peor among the other Baals and traces the occasion to Balaam's advice that the women of Moab draw Israel first into fornication and then into idolatry; on Phinehas he has him rising when no one else would and taking on himself a magistrate's office, and is careful that the commendation is not of justifying righteousness, since no works of the best of men can justify, much less one action, but of a deed God esteemed righteous and sealed with the covenant of a perpetual priesthood. At the waters of strife he insists the fault was not Moses' only but belonged to those who provoked him, which is why it is mentioned.

Clarke records the ancient renderings of the idol's name and takes the sacrifices of the dead for sacrifices of dead men, since most heathen idols were men deified after death and many of them execrated in life; at the waters of strife he reads the two Hebrew words for Moses' lapse as meaning that he stammered, transported with anger. Wesley makes the despising of the land a preference for Egypt and the old bondage, and says the act of Phinehas was accepted and rewarded as one of justice and piety.

Spurgeon locates the root of the contempt for the land in the unbelief that follows it, holding that if we do not believe the Lord's word we shall think lightly of his promised gifts, and that to prefer earthly things to heavenly is to prefer Egypt to Canaan. At Baal-peor he leaves open whether they joined in rites meant to open correspondence with departed spirits, but draws a different moral, that a false way of worship leads before long to a false god, and names the ritualism of his own day as the first step. At the waters of strife he asks whether they will never have done, since the scene changes while the sin continues and the repetition of an old mutiny made the offence sevenfold; but he is gentle with Moses, wearied out after forty years and hopeless of their improving, whose temper gave way — and can we wonder, since he was man and not God.

debates.question: What are the sacrifices of the dead?

positions.view: Sacrifices of dead men, since most heathen idols were men deified after death, many of them execrated while they lived.
Sacrifices of a dead divinity, Baal-peor himself; the parallel is the phrase used elsewhere of the carcases of idols, and no rite for the departed need be sought.
Possibly necromantic rites meant to open correspondence with departed spirits, though the surer lesson is that a false way of worship leads to a false god.
The occasion matters more than the rite: Balaam's counsel that the women of Moab draw Israel into fornication and so into idolatry.

debates.question: Whose spirit was provoked at the waters of strife?

positions.view: God's, on the usage of the phrase, though the natural sense and the ancient versions give Moses'; and the usual account of his offence is in any case partial.
Moses', who though the meekest of men was provoked into passionate and undue expressions — and the provokers share the fault.
Moses', brought into a rebellious and soured state so that he stammered, transported with anger.
Moses', wearied out after forty years and hopeless of their improving; can we wonder, since he was man and not God.

outliers.note: Treats the twenty-seventh verse as copied from a prophet with the source's verb altered, and dates the alteration by noting that it is already present in the Greek version.
Makes the worship of Baal-peor the end of a road that begins in a false manner of worship, and names the ritualism of his own day as the first step on it.

themes: Yea, they despised the pleasant land, they believed not his word:
But murmured in their tents, and hearkened not unto the voice of the Lord.
Therefore he lifted up his hand against them, to overthrow them in the wilderness:
To overthrow their seed also among the nations, and to scatter them in the lands.
They joined themselves also unto Baal–peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead.
Thus they provoked him to anger with their inventions: and the plague brake in upon them.
Then stood up Phinehas, and executed judgment: and so the plague was stayed.
And that was counted unto him for righteousness unto all generations for evermore.
They angered him also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes:
Because they provoked his spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his lips.

34.pericope_label: They did not destroy the nations, concerning whom the LORD commanded them... Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting: and let all the people say, Amen. Praise ye the LORD

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the word rendered devils to mean lords, chosen to carry the sense of the heathen divine names, and traces its Arabic cognate to the title that became the Cid in Spain and survives in the Moorish word for my lord; he notes that child sacrifice was inherent in Canaanite and Phoenician practice, Carthage being notorious for it two centuries after Christ, glosses the pity of their captors as literally giving them for companions, and reads the quotation of the closing doxology in Chronicles as evidence that the book was complete by then. Delitzsch treats the prayer near the end as the goal toward which the whole psalm has struggled by way of self-accusation and praise of God's faithfulness, reads the rare verb that closes it as accounting ourselves happy to be able to praise him, and describes the chronicler as a writer who joins passages like mosaic-work, inserting an indispensable rivet and turning the direction that all the people say Amen into a historical statement that they said it.

Gill traces the mixing through covenants, trade and intermarriage, noting the irony that they came to serve the idols of the very people dispossessed for serving them; he collects the philology of the word for devils without deciding, reporting a derivation from a root meaning to waste and destroy, a rabbinic objection that this needs different pointing, and a proposal from an Arabic root meaning to rule. He fills the history in from Judges on both sides, and is exact about which covenant is remembered — not theirs, who promised to do all the Lord commanded and did not, but his.

Clarke renders the word for idols as their labours or griefs, named from the pains of making the images, the labour of worshipping them and the grief the judgments brought; he insists that the devil is never plural in Scripture, there being one devil though many demons; he reads the kindled wrath as a fire answering that with which they had inflamed themselves before their idols, calls Judges a history of this people's rebellions and deliverances, and renders the closing phrase as from the hidden term to the hidden term, quoting an old psalter: without beginning and without ending. Wesley reads the devils plainly, that they did not worship God as they pretended but the evil spirits supposed to inhabit the images.

Henry marks the transition, that the mercies which settled them in Canaan made no more durable impression than those that fetched them out of Egypt, and that the first step of apostasy was sparing the nations under a pretence of pity. Spurgeon is harsher about the motive — sloth, cowardice or sinful complacency sheathed the sword too soon — and applies it to partial sanctification, since we make alliances of peace where we ought to proclaim war to the knife; at the turn he finds it very godlike that the Lord did not shut out the prayer of those who had shut their ears against him, his fiercest wrath toward his own people being a temporary flame while his love burns on for ever.

debates.question: What is the word rendered devils?

positions.view: Demons, and the number matters: the devil is never plural in Scripture, there being one devil though many demons.
Literally lords, the word chosen to render the heathen divine names, its Arabic cognate surviving in the Moorish title for my lord.
The evil spirits supposed by the heathen to inhabit their images, so that the worship was of devils and not of God.
Undecided: a root meaning to waste and destroy, a rabbinic objection to that derivation, and an Arabic root meaning to rule are all reported.

debates.question: What does the closing doxology show about the Psalter?

positions.view: That the fourth book was already complete, if not the whole collection, since the doxology is quoted as part of the psalm in Chronicles.
That the chronicler worked like a mosaicist, inserting a rivet to join the psalm's beginning to its end and converting the liturgical direction into a historical clause.
Not a question of formation but of language: from everlasting to everlasting is from the hidden term to the hidden term, without beginning and without ending.
A call rather than evidence: should all the nations unite in the acclaim it would still fall short of what is deserved.

outliers.note: Turns the failure to exterminate the nations into a charge of partial sanctification, saying that we make alliances of peace where we ought to proclaim war to the knife, and plead temperament, habit or circumstance as an excuse.
Follows the Hebrew word for the false gods into Arabic and thence into the Spanish title of the Cid and the Moorish word for my lord.

themes: They did not destroy the nations, concerning whom the Lord commanded them:
But were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works.
And they served their idols: which were a snare unto them.
Yea, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils,
And shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: and the land was polluted with blood.
Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions.
Therefore was the wrath of the Lord kindled against his people, insomuch that he abhorred his own inheritance.
And he gave them into the hand of the heathen; and they that hated them ruled over them.
Their enemies also oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their hand.
Many times did he deliver them; but they provoked him with their counsel, and were brought low for their iniquity.
Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry:
And he remembered for them his covenant, and repented according to the multitude of his mercies.
He made them also to be pitied of all those that carried them captives.
Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the heathen, to give thanks unto thy holy name, and to triumph in thy praise.
Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting: and let all the people say, Amen. Praise ye the Lord.
